                                  SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                     PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
 JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR           §                                         BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
 ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY            §
 LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION            §                                         OF
 SERVICES CORPORATION TO              §
 AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF          §                                         ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
 CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY            §
 FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST             §
 SWITCH TO BIG HILL                   §
 SUBSTATION 765-KV                    §
 TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN         §
 BELL, BURNET, CONCHO,                §
 CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO,
 MASON, MCCULLOCH, MENARD,
 MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,
 SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND
 WILLIAMSON COUNTIES
                  MARK ALLAN BRADBURY'S REPLY BRIEF REGARDING
                   REMANDED PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 11 AND 13
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
COMES NOW Mark Allan Bradbury, pro se Intervenor, and files this Reply Brief regarding the
Commission's remand of Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13. This reply addresses the Applicants'
September 21, 2026 Directory of Record Evidence, PUC Interchange Item No. 6593, and the record-
based arguments presented in the other uploaded remand filings. The remand does not reopen the case
or relieve Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation
(Applicants) of their burden of proof. It asks SOAH to answer two questions the original PFD did not
expressly answer. The existing record supports direct answers: Applicants did not establish that Import
Path 2 is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, and they did not establish a quantified
estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable to these proposed facilities. SOAH should
preserve its original assessment of the evidence and again recommend denial of the CCN.

I. THE REMAND IS LIMITED AND DOES NOT CHANGE APPLICANTS' BURDEN
The Commission's remand order identifies only two omitted Preliminary Order issues: Issue 11—
whether the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability
standards—and Issue 13—the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from
the proposed facilities, considering current and future congestion and the facilities' ability to reduce it.
The Commission directed SOAH to fully address those issues in a supplemental or amended PFD.
Order Remanding Proceeding to SOAH, Item No. 6578, at 2-3.
Applicants respond with a 22-page 'Directory' collecting favorable excerpts from the PBRP, the 2024
and 2025 RTP materials, rebuttal testimony, and other evidence. Item No. 6593. But a collection of
conclusions does not supply the missing analytical link. The relevant question under Issue 11 is not
whether ERCOT identified regional reliability concerns, or whether ERCOT recommended a 765-kV
portfolio. It is whether Applicants proved that these proposed Import Path 2 facilities are necessary to
meet an identified state or federal reliability standard. Likewise, Issue 13 asks for an estimate of
consumer congestion cost savings from these facilities, not historical ERCOT-wide congestion rent or
statewide portfolio economics.
Aaron Howton correctly frames the remand: the supplemental findings should identify the reliability
standard, the study case and data producing the violation, and the analysis demonstrating how Import

                             Bradbury Reply Brief — Remanded Issues 11 and 13   Page 1
 Path 2 cures that violation; if a factual link is absent, the PFD should say so rather than infer it from
the project's classification. Item No. 6584 at 3-5. The Mewhinney Family makes the same point in
greater detail, explaining that Applicants cannot discharge their burden by treating selection in an
integrated regional plan as proof of project-specific necessity. Item No. 6617 at 3-4.

II. ISSUE 11: APPLICANTS DID NOT PROVE THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS NECESSARY TO MEET A
RELIABILITY STANDARD
A. ERCOT studied multiple voltage alternatives that met the reliability criteria.
Applicants emphasize that ERCOT performed reliability assessments under NERC Reliability
Standard TPL-001-5.1, ERCOT Protocols, and ERCOT Planning Criteria, and that the study observed
thermal and voltage violations, instability, and unsolved power flows. Item No. 6593 at 3-14. That
evidence establishes that ERCOT identified a regional planning problem. It does not establish that this
particular 765-kV project is the only—or necessary—means of satisfying the applicable standards.
The contrary record evidence is especially important. The Mewhinney Family identifies PBRP Table
7.6 as showing that the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import-path alternatives each meet ERCOT and
NERC reliability criteria. Item No. 6617 at 4-5. If multiple materially different transmission portfolios
satisfy the same reliability criteria, Applicants cannot prove the necessity of the requested 765-kV
Import Path 2 merely by showing that the selected portfolio also complies. Compliance by a selected
plan is not the same as necessity of the particular facilities for compliance.
B. Applicants do not tie a specific TPL-001-5.1 violation to the necessity of this line.
Applicants' Directory lists the contingency categories and performance limits ERCOT applied,
including P0, P1, P2, P3, P5, P6 and P7 conditions, thermal ratings, voltage limits, and dynamic-
stability criteria. Item No. 6593 at 3-5. Yet the Directory does not identify, for each asserted violation,
the modeled condition that fails without Import Path 2 and the record analysis showing that the Bell
County East-to-Big Hill facilities are necessary to cure that specific failure.
Indeed, Applicants quote Mr. Gurley's cross-examination acknowledging that he was not aware of a
study that isolated each import-path line independently because the lines were studied together. Item
No. 6593 at 13. That admission is significant. Issue 11 concerns 'the proposed transmission facilities.'
A portfolio study showing that multiple facilities collectively improve system performance does not,
without more, establish that this individual CCN is necessary to meet the identified reliability
standard.
C. Giving ERCOT's recommendation great weight does not make it conclusive.
Applicants repeatedly invoke the requirement to give ERCOT's recommendation great weight. Item
No. 6593 at 3, 8-14. But 'great weight' is still evidentiary weight; it does not convert ERCOT's
recommendation into an irrebuttable presumption or eliminate SOAH's obligation to weigh contrary
evidence. The Mewhinney brief notes that the original PFD made an alternative determination against
the recommendation even when great weight was afforded to it. Item No. 6617 at 6-7, 13.
Nor can repetition of the recommendation cure disputed inputs. The PBRP, later RTPs, and later
presentations may repeat or incorporate the 765-kV core plan, but the fact that a planning assumption
is carried forward does not independently validate the load forecast, generation assumptions, timing,
or project-specific need on which the original recommendation depended.




                            Bradbury Reply Brief — Remanded Issues 11 and 13   Page 2
 D. The record does not reconcile Central Texas load with the assumed westward transfers.
The Mewhinney Family identifies Applicants' discovery responses showing that neither Oncor nor
ERCOT performed the requested analysis parsing Central Texas's net generation position or the effect
of concurrent Central Texas data-center demand on generation otherwise assumed available for
westward export. Item No. 6617 at 8-9. The same filing notes that Applicants were unaware of the
requested sensitivity scenario having been studied by ERCOT. Id.
Those omissions matter because Import Path 2 is premised on moving large quantities of power across
Central Texas toward the Permian Basin. If the record does not establish the generation available for
that transfer after serving growing Central Texas load, the asserted necessity of the line cannot be
inferred simply from its inclusion in a statewide plan.
E. The record does not adequately reconcile the original PBRP forecast with later forecasting
changes.
The remand record also preserves a substantial forecast problem. The Mewhinney brief explains that
the original PBRP's extra-high-voltage analysis was focused on 2038 and that the record contains
contrary evidence concerning the timing of Import Path 2, including ERCOT's December 12, 2024
sequencing letter prioritizing two other import paths for 2030. Item No. 6617 at 9-10.
More fundamentally, the PFD evidence summarized in Item 6617 identifies Applicants' failure to
reanalyze the PBRP forecast under ERCOT's later adjusted realization methodology, as well as the
absence of evidence that ERCOT validated the oil-and-gas projections underlying the original study.
Item No. 6617 at 10-12. Applicants' Directory responds largely by pointing to later studies that
continue to include the 765-kV plan. Item No. 6593 at 8-12. Continued inclusion is not a quantitative
reconciliation of the changed forecast.
F. Later Far West constraints do not prove the necessity of this specific CCN.
Applicants cite the North-to-Far-West and South-to-Far-West Generic Transmission Constraints and
assert that the Permian 765-kV import paths are critical elements of ERCOT's exit strategy. Item No.
6593 at 11-13. That evidence may show a broader operational benefit from additional transfer
capability. It still does not identify a state or federal reliability standard that requires this particular
segment, nor does it cure the absence of an isolated analysis of Import Path 2.
A regional need for additional service is not synonymous with necessity of every proposed element of
a regional portfolio. The Commission remanded Issue 11 precisely so SOAH could answer whether
these facilities are necessary to meet the standards. The answer should turn on the record evidence
connecting the standard to this project, not on the circular proposition that the project is necessary
because ERCOT selected it.
G. The reliability classification cannot substitute for proof.
John Bradley's reply correctly identifies the logical problem in Applicants' position: Applicants rely on
the project's classification as a reliability project while resisting the project-specific proof demanded
by Issue 11. Item No. 6611 at 2-4. The classification may determine which regulatory pathway
applies, but it does not itself answer the factual question the Commission expressly remanded.
SOAH should therefore expressly find that Applicants have not established that the Bell County East-
to-Big Hill 765-kV facilities are necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard. That finding
is fully consistent with the original PFD's adverse assessment of the need evidence and should support
reaffirmance of the recommendation to deny the CCN.

                             Bradbury Reply Brief — Remanded Issues 11 and 13   Page 3
 III. ISSUE 13: APPLICANTS DID NOT ESTABLISH CONSUMER CONGESTION COST SAVINGS
ATTRIBUTABLE TO THESE FACILITIES
A. Applicants cite statewide and portfolio figures, not a project-specific estimate.
Applicants' Issue 13 directory begins with ERCOT-wide historical congestion rent—$2.3 billion in
2023 and $1.97 billion in 2024—and statewide comparisons between the complete 765-kV STEP and
the 345-kV plan. Item No. 6593 at 15-18. Those numbers describe the ERCOT system or entire
transmission portfolios. They do not quantify consumer congestion cost savings attributable to the
Bell County East-to-Big Hill segment.
The Mewhinney Family explains that the January Comparison adds each complete transmission plan
to statewide economic base cases and reports statewide outcomes without allocating the results to
Import Path 2. Item No. 6617 at 14-15. The 2025 RTP materials likewise begin with the 765-kV STEP
already included. Id. at 15. A model that assumes the project as part of a complete installed portfolio
cannot, without an incremental calculation, identify the amount of savings caused by this CCN.
B. Historical congestion rent is not the requested savings estimate.
Historical ERCOT-wide congestion rent establishes that congestion exists. It does not answer how
much congestion this project will relieve, in what years, under what load and generation assumptions,
or how much of any reduction will benefit consumers. Item No. 6617 at 15-16. Issue 13 asks for
estimated savings that 'may result from the proposed transmission facilities.' The word 'result' requires
a causal, project-linked estimate, not a description of past system congestion.
C. The statewide 765-kV-versus-345-kV comparison cannot be assigned to Import Path 2.
Applicants cite the statewide 765-kV STEP comparison as showing long-term production-cost and
consumer-energy-cost advantages over the 345-kV plan. Item No. 6593 at 15-18. Even accepting
those portfolio figures, the record does not provide a supported method for allocating them to Import
Path 2 by mileage, construction cost, number of import paths, or any other causal measure. Item No.
6617 at 14-16.
The problem is reinforced by the modeled results themselves. The Mewhinney Family notes that, for
2034, ERCOT's statewide comparison reports $136 million less consumer energy cost savings for the
765-kV portfolio than for the 345-kV portfolio. Item No. 6617 at 15. That does not establish that the
765-kV portfolio lacks other benefits; it does show why Applicants cannot characterize a portfolio
comparison as an unqualified, project-specific consumer-savings estimate.
D. Production cost, consumer energy cost, and congestion rent are distinct metrics.
The economic tables cited on remand report different outputs, including production costs, consumer
energy costs, and congestion rent. Item No. 6617 at 15. Applicants cannot treat those measures as
interchangeable without record evidence explaining the relationship, avoiding double counting, and
demonstrating what portion constitutes congestion cost savings to consumers attributable to these
facilities.
Nor does the project's reliability classification excuse the missing answer. The Commission expressly
remanded Issue 13. As Howton explains, if SOAH concludes the facilities are not shown necessary to
meet reliability standards, PURA § 37.056(d) makes the economic comparison consequential; the
existing PFD found that the record contained no evidence quantifying the consumer congestion
savings and no estimated project cost to consumers. Item No. 6584 at 4-5.


                            Bradbury Reply Brief — Remanded Issues 11 and 13   Page 4
 E. The proper answer to Issue 13 is that the amount is not established in the record.
SOAH need not invent a number to answer the remand. It should state directly that Applicants did not
establish a quantified estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable to the proposed
Import Path 2 facilities. That is an answer to Issue 13, and it accurately describes the evidentiary
record. The absence of the required project-specific estimate cannot be cured by substituting statewide
historical totals or full-portfolio comparisons.

IV. APPLICANTS' DIRECTORY DOES NOT CURE THE ORIGINAL NEED DEFECTS
Applicants' Directory is useful in one respect: it demonstrates the difference between evidence that
ERCOT studied a regional problem and evidence that this project is necessary. The Directory contains
extensive quotations establishing that ERCOT used reliability criteria, identified regional violations,
evaluated portfolios, recommended multiple import paths, and later incorporated the 765-kV core plan
into other planning work. Item No. 6593. But the critical gaps remain.
 • Applicants do not identify a study isolating Import Path 2 and proving that a specified reliability
   violation persists without it;
 • the record shows multiple voltage alternatives were modeled as meeting the applicable reliability
    criteria;
 • the record does not adequately reconcile the original load assumptions with later forecasting
    methodology and changed demand evidence;
 • the record does not adequately establish the generation available for westward transfer after
    concurrent Central Texas load is served; and
 • the record contains no quantified estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable
    specifically to these proposed facilities.
These are not peripheral objections. They are the factual links required to answer the two questions the
Commission remanded. The supplemental PFD should not fill them by inference.

V. REQUESTED FINDINGS ON REMAND
Intervenor respectfully requests that the supplemental PFD expressly find: (1) ERCOT identified
regional reliability concerns and evaluated the PBRP under NERC and ERCOT planning criteria; (2)
the record does not establish that the Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kV facilities, considered as the
facilities before the Commission in this CCN, are necessary to meet a specified state or federal
reliability standard; (3) the record does not contain a study isolating Import Path 2 and demonstrating
that the identified reliability violation cannot be resolved without these facilities; (4) the record
reflects materially different transmission voltage alternatives that ERCOT identified as satisfying the
applicable reliability criteria; (5) the record does not establish a quantified estimate of consumer
congestion cost savings attributable to these proposed facilities; and (6) statewide congestion-rent
figures and full-portfolio economic comparisons do not establish the project-specific amount
requested by Preliminary Order Issue 13.
Those findings lead to the same ultimate result as the original PFD. Applicants have not carried their
burden to establish that the requested CCN is necessary. The absence of a project-specific reliability
showing under Issue 11 and the absence of a project-specific consumer congestion-savings estimate
under Issue 13 reinforce, rather than undermine, SOAH's original recommendation.



                            Bradbury Reply Brief — Remanded Issues 11 and 13   Page 5
 VI. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
The Commission did not remand this case to permit Applicants to replace the evidentiary record with
a planning label or a collection of statewide portfolio conclusions. It remanded because Issues 11 and
13 require express answers. On the closed record, those answers are straightforward.
Applicants proved that ERCOT identified serious regional planning challenges and selected a 765-kV
portfolio. They did not prove that these particular facilities are necessary to meet a specified state or
federal reliability standard, and they did not prove the amount of consumer congestion cost savings
attributable to these facilities. Accordingly, Mark Allan Bradbury respectfully requests that the
Administrative Law Judges issue a supplemental PFD answering Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13
adversely to Applicants, preserve and reaffirm the original recommendation, and recommend that the
Public Utility Commission of Texas DENY the application for a Certificate of Convenience and
Necessity in PUC Docket No. 59475.

Respectfully submitted,

__________________________________
Mark Allan Bradbury
Pro Se Intervenor
504 Grand Ave. Brady, TX 76825
972-742-7116
bradburyma@yahoo.com

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE
I certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing was served on all parties of record in accordance
with the applicable orders and rules governing service in SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349 and PUC
Docket No. 59475 on Oct 7th, 2026.

__________________________________
Mark Allan Bradbury

IV. APPLICANTS' DIRECTORY DOES NOT CURE THE ORIGINAL NEED DEFECTS
Applicants' Directory is useful in one respect: it demonstrates the difference between evidence that
ERCOT studied a regional problem and evidence that this project is necessary. The Directory contains
extensive quotations establishing that ERCOT used reliability criteria, identified regional violations,
evaluated portfolios, recommended multiple import paths, and later incorporated the 765-kV core plan
into other planning work. Item No. 6593. But the critical gaps remain.
 • Applicants do not identify a study isolating Import Path 2 and proving that a specified reliability
   violation persists without it;
 • the record shows multiple voltage alternatives were modeled as meeting the applicable reliability
    criteria;
 • the record does not adequately reconcile the original load assumptions with later forecasting
    methodology and changed demand evidence;
 • the record does not adequately establish the generation available for westward transfer after
    concurrent Central Texas load is served; and
 • the record contains no quantified estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable
    specifically to these proposed facilities.
These are not peripheral objections. They are the factual links required to answer the two questions the
Commission remanded. The supplemental PFD should not fill them by inference.

V. REQUESTED FINDINGS ON REMAND
Intervenor respectfully requests that the supplemental PFD expressly find: (1) ERCOT identified
regional reliability concerns and evaluated the PBRP under NERC and ERCOT planning criteria; (2)
the record does not establish that the Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kV facilities, considered as the
facilities before the Commission in this CCN, are necessary to meet a specified state or federal
reliability standard; (3) the record does not contain a study isolating Import Path 2 and demonstrating
that the identified reliability violation cannot be resolved without these facilities; (4) the record
reflects materially different transmission voltage alternatives that ERCOT identified as satisfying the
applicable reliability criteria; (5) the record does not establish a quantified estimate of consumer
congestion cost savings attributable to these proposed facilities; and (6) statewide congestion-rent
figures and full-portfolio economic comparisons do not establish the project-specific amount
requested by Preliminary Order Issue 13.
Those findings lead to the same ultimate result as the original PFD. Applicants have not carried their
burden to establish that the requested CCN is necessary. The absence of a project-specific reliability
showing under Issue 11 and the absence of a project-specific consumer congestion-savings estimate
under Issue 13 reinforce, rather than undermine, SOAH's original recommendation.
